entities.label: the young lady at the bazaar stall
the two young gentlemen with English accents
the weary-looking man at the turnstile
the two men counting money on a salver
the porcelain vases and flowered tea-sets
the great jars like eastern guards
the boy's house (the priest's former house)
the back drawing-room where the priest died
the special train to the bazaar

occurrences.description: North Richmond Street, being blind, is quiet except when the Christian Brothers' School sets the boys free; an uninhabited house stands at the blind end and the other houses gaze at one another with brown imperturbable faces.
occurrences.quote:
North Richmond Street, being blind, was a quiet street except at the
hour when the Christian Brothers’ School set the boys free.

occurrences.description: The former tenant of the house, a priest, died in the back drawing-room; in his will he left his money to institutions and his furniture to his sister.
occurrences.quote:
The former tenant of our house, a priest, had died in the back
drawing-room.

occurrences.description: In the waste room behind the kitchen the boy finds a few paper-covered books: The Abbot, The Devout Communicant and The Memoirs of Vidocq; he likes the last best because its leaves are yellow.
occurrences.quote:
Among these I found a few paper-covered books, the
pages of which were curled and damp

occurrences.description: In the wild garden behind the house, under a straggling bush, the boy finds the late tenant's rusty bicycle-pump.
occurrences.quote:
under one of
which I found the late tenant’s rusty bicycle-pump

occurrences.description: In the short days of winter the boys play in the street after dusk until their bodies glow, running through dark muddy lanes past the rough tribes from the cottages, the ashpits and the dark odorous stables.
occurrences.quote:
The
cold air stung us and we played till our bodies glowed.

occurrences.description: If the uncle is seen turning the corner, the boys hide in the shadow until they have seen him safely housed.
occurrences.quote:
If my uncle was seen turning the
corner we hid in the shadow until we had seen him safely housed.

occurrences.description: When Mangan's sister comes out on the doorstep to call her brother in to his tea, the boys watch her from their shadow peer up and down the street.
occurrences.quote:
Mangan’s sister came out on the doorstep to call her brother in to his
tea we watched her from our shadow peer up and down the street

occurrences.description: While her brother teases her before obeying, the boy stands by the railings looking at her; her dress swings as she moves and the soft rope of her hair tosses from side to side, her figure defined by the light from the half-opened door.
occurrences.quote:
Her dress swung as she moved her body and the
soft rope of her hair tossed from side to side.

occurrences.description: Every morning the boy lies on the floor in the front parlour watching her door, the blind pulled down to within an inch of the sash so that he cannot be seen.
occurrences.quote:
Every morning I lay on the floor in the front parlour watching her
door.

occurrences.description: When she comes out, the boy seizes his books and follows her, keeping her brown figure always in his eye; near the point where their ways diverge he quickens his pace and passes her. This happens morning after morning; he has never spoken to her except for a few casual words.
occurrences.quote:
I kept her brown
figure always in my eye

occurrences.description: On Saturday evenings the boy carries parcels for his aunt through the flaring streets, jostled by drunken men and bargaining women, amid curses of labourers, shrill litanies of shop-boys and the nasal chanting of street-singers singing a come-all-you about O'Donovan Rossa or a ballad about the troubles in our native land.
occurrences.quote:
We walked through the flaring streets, jostled by
drunken men and bargaining women

occurrences.description: Amid the market noises the boy imagines that he bears his chalice safely through a throng of foes; her name springs to his lips in strange prayers and praises which he himself does not understand.
occurrences.quote:
I
imagined that I bore my chalice safely through a throng of foes.

occurrences.description: The boy's eyes are often full of tears, he cannot tell why, and at times a flood from his heart seems to pour itself out into his bosom; his body is like a harp and her words and gestures like fingers running upon the wires.
occurrences.quote:
my body was like a harp
and her words and gestures were like fingers running upon the wires

occurrences.description: One dark rainy evening the boy goes into the back drawing-room where the priest died; hearing rain on the sodden beds through a broken pane, he presses his palms together until they tremble, murmuring 'O love! O love!' many times.
occurrences.quote:
I pressed
the palms of my hands together until they trembled, murmuring: _“O
love! O love!”_ many times.

occurrences.description: At last she speaks to him, asking was he going to Araby; he forgets whether he answered yes or no. It would be a splendid bazaar, she says; she would love to go.
occurrences.quote:
She asked me was I
going to _Araby_.

occurrences.description: The boy asks her, 'And why can't you?'
occurrences.quote: “And why can’t you?” I asked.

occurrences.description: While she speaks she turns a silver bracelet round and round her wrist; she cannot go because there will be a retreat that week in her convent. Her brother and two other boys are fighting for their caps and the boy is alone at the railings.
occurrences.quote: While she spoke she turned a silver bracelet round and round her wrist.

occurrences.description: She holds one of the spikes, bowing her head towards him; the light from the lamp opposite catches the white curve of her neck, lights up her hair and the hand upon the railing, and catches the white border of a petticoat, just visible as she stands at ease.
occurrences.quote:
The light from the lamp opposite our door
caught the white curve of her neck

occurrences.description: She says, 'It's well for you.'
occurrences.quote: “It’s well for you,” she said.

occurrences.description: The boy says, 'If I go, I will bring you something.'
occurrences.quote: “If I go,” I said, “I will bring you something.”

occurrences.description: After that evening the boy wishes to annihilate the tedious intervening days; her image comes between him and the page he strives to read, and the syllables of the word Araby are called to him through the silence.
occurrences.quote:
The syllables of the word _Araby_ were called to me through
the silence in which my soul luxuriated

occurrences.description: The boy asks for leave to go to the bazaar on Saturday night; his aunt is surprised and hopes it is not some Freemason affair.
occurrences.quote:
I asked for leave to go to the bazaar on Saturday night. My
aunt was surprised and hoped it was not some Freemason affair.

occurrences.description: The boy answers few questions in class; he watches his master's face pass from amiability to sternness, the master hoping he is not beginning to idle.
occurrences.quote:
I watched my master’s face pass from
amiability to sternness

occurrences.description: On Saturday morning the boy reminds his uncle that he wishes to go to the bazaar in the evening; the uncle, fussing at the hallstand for the hat-brush, answers curtly: 'Yes, boy, I know.'
occurrences.quote:
On Saturday morning I reminded my uncle that I wished to go to the
bazaar in the evening.

occurrences.description: Unable to lie at the parlour window because the uncle is in the hall, the boy leaves the house in bad humour and walks slowly towards the school through pitilessly raw air.
occurrences.quote:
I left the house in bad humour and walked slowly towards
the school.

occurrences.description: The uncle not yet home at dinner, the boy mounts to the high cold empty gloomy rooms of the upper house and goes from room to room singing; from the front window he watches his companions playing below and looks over at the dark house where she lives, seeing the brown-clad figure cast by his imagination.
occurrences.quote:
The high cold empty gloomy rooms
liberated me and I went from room to room singing.

occurrences.description: Downstairs the boy finds Mrs Mercer, an old garrulous pawnbroker's widow who collects used stamps for some pious purpose, sitting at the fire; he endures the gossip of the tea-table, the meal prolonged beyond an hour, and still the uncle does not come.
occurrences.quote:
I found Mrs Mercer sitting at the fire.
She was an old garrulous woman, a pawnbroker’s widow

occurrences.description: Mrs Mercer stands up to go after eight o'clock, sorry she cannot wait, as the night air is bad for her; the boy begins to walk up and down the room, clenching his fists, and his aunt says, 'I'm afraid you may put off your bazaar for this night of Our Lord.'
occurrences.quote: “I’m afraid you may put off your bazaar for this night of Our Lord.”

occurrences.description: At nine o'clock the boy hears his uncle's latchkey in the halldoor, hears him talking to himself and the hallstand rocking under the weight of his overcoat; the boy can interpret these signs.
occurrences.quote: At nine o’clock I heard my uncle’s latchkey in the halldoor.

occurrences.description: Midway through his dinner the boy asks the uncle for the money to go to the bazaar; the uncle has forgotten, and says, 'The people are in bed and after their first sleep now.'
occurrences.quote:
When he was midway through his dinner I asked him to give me the money
to go to the bazaar. He had forgotten.

occurrences.description: The boy does not smile; his aunt says energetically, 'Can't you give him the money and let him go? You've kept him late enough as it is.'
occurrences.quote:
“Can’t you give him the money and let him go? You’ve kept him late
enough as it is.”

occurrences.description: The uncle says he is very sorry he forgot and that he believes in the old saying 'All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy'; told a second time where the boy is going, he asks did he know 'The Arab's Farewell to his Steed' and, as the boy leaves the kitchen, is about to recite its opening lines to the aunt.
occurrences.quote:
he
asked me did I know _The Arab’s Farewell to his Steed_

occurrences.description: The boy holds a florin tightly in his hand as he strides down Buckingham Street towards the station; the streets thronged with buyers and glaring with gas recall to him the purpose of his journey.
occurrences.quote:
I held a florin tightly in my hand as I strode down Buckingham Street
towards the station.

occurrences.description: The boy takes his seat in a third-class carriage of a deserted train, which after an intolerable delay creeps out among ruinous houses and over the twinkling river; at Westland Row porters keep a crowd back, saying it is a special train for the bazaar, and he remains alone in the bare carriage.
occurrences.quote:
I took my
seat in a third-class carriage of a deserted train.

occurrences.description: The train draws up beside an improvised wooden platform; the boy passes out onto the road, sees by a lighted clock-dial that it is ten minutes to ten, and before him a large building displays the magical name.
occurrences.quote:
In front of me was a large building which displayed the magical
name.

occurrences.description: Finding no sixpenny entrance and fearing the bazaar will close, the boy passes in quickly through a turnstile, handing a shilling to a weary-looking man.
occurrences.quote:
I passed in quickly through a turnstile, handing a
shilling to a weary-looking man.

occurrences.description: The boy finds himself in a big hall girdled at half its height by a gallery; nearly all the stalls are closed, the greater part of the hall is in darkness, and he recognises a silence like that which pervades a church after a service.
occurrences.quote:
I recognised a silence
like that which pervades a church after a service.

occurrences.description: Before a curtain over which the words Café Chantant are written in coloured lamps, two men count money on a salver; the boy listens to the fall of the coins.
occurrences.quote:
two men were counting
money on a salver. I listened to the fall of the coins.

occurrences.description: Remembering with difficulty why he had come, the boy goes over to one of the open stalls and examines porcelain vases and flowered tea-sets.
occurrences.quote:
I went over to one of the
stalls and examined porcelain vases and flowered tea-sets.

occurrences.description: At the door of the stall a young lady is talking and laughing with two young gentlemen; the boy remarks their English accents and listens vaguely to their conversation, which ends 'O, there's a ... fib!'
occurrences.quote:
I remarked their English accents and listened vaguely to
their conversation.

occurrences.description: Observing him, the young lady comes over and asks did he wish to buy anything; the tone of her voice is not encouraging, as if she has spoken out of a sense of duty.
occurrences.quote:
Observing me the young lady came over and asked me did I wish to buy
anything.

occurrences.description: Looking humbly at the great jars that stand like eastern guards at either side of the dark entrance to the stall, the boy murmurs, 'No, thank you.'
occurrences.quote:
I looked humbly at the great jars
that stood like eastern guards at either side of the dark entrance to
the stall

occurrences.description: The young lady changes the position of one of the vases and goes back to the two young men; they talk of the same subject, and once or twice she glances at the boy over her shoulder.
occurrences.quote:
The young lady changed the position of one of the vases and went back
to the two young men.

occurrences.description: The boy lingers before the stall though he knows his stay is useless, then turns away slowly and walks down the middle of the bazaar, allowing the two pennies to fall against the sixpence in his pocket.
occurrences.quote:
I allowed the two pennies to
fall against the sixpence in my pocket.

occurrences.description: A voice calls from one end of the gallery that the light is out; the upper part of the hall is now completely dark.
occurrences.quote:
I heard a voice call from one
end of the gallery that the light was out.

occurrences.description: Gazing up into the darkness the boy sees himself as a creature driven and derided by vanity, and his eyes burn with anguish and anger.
occurrences.quote:
I saw myself as a creature driven and
derided by vanity; and my eyes burned with anguish and anger.

boy.subject: char:mangans-sister
boy.to: a figure defined by light, wholly radiant, worth every evening of watching

boy.subject: char:boy
boy.to: when her door opens my heart leaps; her name springs to my lips in prayers I do not understand

boy.subject: place:market-streets
boy.to: a place most hostile to romance, a throng of foes to be passed through unharmed

boy.subject: char:boy
boy.to: a bearer of a sacred chalice, guarding something holy through the crowd

boy.subject: char:boy
boy.to: prayers and praises rise from me unbidden; my body is a harp she plays upon

boy.subject: char:boy
boy.to: devotion so intense that all my senses desire to veil themselves

boy.subject: char:mangans-sister
boy.to: she has spoken to me at last; the whole world is changed by her words

boy.subject: char:mangans-sister
boy.to: the lamplight itself serves her, lighting her neck, her hair, her hand

boy.subject: char:boy
boy.to: a vow undertaken: I will go to Araby and bring her something worthy of her

boy.subject: place:araby-bazaar
boy.to: a splendid place whose very syllables cast an Eastern enchantment over my soul

boy.subject: char:boy
boy.to: chafing against school; the serious work of life is ugly monotonous child's play beside my desire

boy.subject: char:boy
boy.to: liberated by the high cold empty rooms, singing, her image touched discreetly by lamplight

boy.subject: char:boy
boy.to: the delay is intolerable; every minute the uncle eats is stolen from the quest

boy.subject: object:florin
boy.to: the token of the quest, gripped tightly, purpose recalled by its weight

boy.subject: place:araby-bazaar
boy.to: the magical name displayed at last; the enchanted place reached

boy.subject: char:boy
boy.to: a creature driven and derided by vanity

boy.subject: char:boy
boy.to: anguish and anger; the enchantment gone out in the dark, nothing bought, nothing to bring her

boy.subject: char:boy
boy.to: what did I ever want from that bazaar? there was nothing there I could have brought her

boy.subject: char:boy
boy.to: no quest — an errand I dressed up as one; I had hardly ever even spoken to her

boy.subject: char:boy
boy.to: my prayers were to nobody; I made a religion of a girl at a railing

narrator.subject: place:north-richmond-street
narrator.to: blind and imperturbable: a dead end wearing a face of decency

narrator.subject: place:back-drawing-room
narrator.to: musty air of a faith long enclosed; the house we lived in was already a reliquary

narrator.subject: char:boy
narrator.to: play already circumscribed by dark lanes, ashpits and shadow; even joy ran a gauntlet

narrator.subject: char:boy
narrator.to: confused adoration beginning, mistaken by the child for devotion

narrator.subject: char:boy
narrator.to: foolish blood, foolish daily rites of watching a door through a lowered blind

narrator.subject: char:boy
narrator.to: romance borrowed wholesale from religion; the child cast himself as grail-bearer in a market street

narrator.subject: char:boy
narrator.to: prayers addressed to no god he could have named; sentiment mistaken for sanctity in a dead priest's room

narrator.subject: char:boy
narrator.to: an errand inflated into a quest by a boy who had never truly spoken to her

narrator.subject: place:araby-bazaar
narrator.to: a name doing work no actual bazaar could do; Eastern enchantment conjured from syllables

narrator.subject: char:uncle
narrator.to: signs the boy could already interpret: the talking to himself, the rocking hallstand

narrator.subject: char:uncle
narrator.to: carelessness dressed up in proverb and recitation; the guardian of the quest could not even remember it

narrator.subject: char:boy
narrator.to: the misgiving heart of that morning confirmed; a deserted special train was the truth of the journey

narrator.subject: place:araby-bazaar
narrator.to: a church after a service: the enchantment already over before the pilgrim arrived

narrator.subject: char:boy
narrator.to: the errand hollow at the very moment of performing it; there was never anything to buy

narrator.subject: char:boy
narrator.to: a creature driven and derided by vanity

narrator.subject: char:boy
narrator.to: anguish and anger: the one moment the child's eyes and mine are the same

narrator.subject: char:mangans-sister
narrator.to: I remember lamplight, a white curve of neck, the border of a petticoat — memory made her an image, never a person; that was the trouble from the start

narrator.subject: char:aunt
narrator.to: her one energetic sentence rescues the errand the uncle forgot; kindness in that house spoke rarely and to the point

reader.subject: place:north-richmond-street
reader.to: a blind street: the dead end is the figure for every route the story will take

reader.subject: char:priest
reader.to: charity itemized in a will: money to institutions, furniture to a sister; piety audited like an estate

reader.subject: object:priests-books
reader.to: devotion, romance and crime fiction shelved together, the yellowest leaves preferred; reading habits the story will repeat

reader.subject: place:market-streets
reader.to: the litanies of shop-boys: liturgy already fused to commerce, sacred vocabulary at the pig-cheek barrels

reader.subject: char:boy
reader.to: religious language doing romantic work; the chalice is borrowed capital he will spend at the bazaar

reader.subject: object:silver-bracelet
reader.to: she turns silver on her wrist while pleading a convent retreat; ornament and piety on the same arm

reader.subject: place:araby-bazaar
reader.to: shabby Orientalism: an Eastern enchantment retailed in Dublin at a shilling a head

reader.subject: char:mrs-mercer
reader.to: a pawnbroker's widow collecting used stamps for a pious purpose: piety and pawnage joined again

reader.subject: char:uncle
reader.to: latchkey signs the boy can interpret: drink, familiar and never named; the household economy of a Dublin Saturday

reader.subject: object:florin
reader.to: two shillings: the entire treasury of the quest, and it will not survive the gate

reader.subject: object:florin
reader.to: half the florin gone to a weary man at the turnstile; no sixpenny entrance for latecomers

reader.subject: place:cafe-chantant
reader.to: coins falling on a salver in church-like silence: the collection plate after the service

reader.subject: char:young-lady
reader.to: English accents flirting over a 'fib' at an Oriental bazaar: the imperial marketplace in miniature, indifferent to Dublin devotion

reader.subject: char:boy
reader.to: with eightpence left he could not have bought her anything anyway; the refusal only ratifies the arithmetic

reader.subject: object:florin
reader.to: two pennies against the sixpence: the audit of the quest, counted out in his pocket

reader.subject: place:araby-bazaar
reader.to: closing time as revelation: the lights go out on the enchantment because the till is counted

reader.subject: char:boy
reader.to: epiphany as anagnorisis: the blind street internalized; Dublin's paralysis recognized from inside a darkened hall

reader.subject: char:mangans-sister
reader.to: the light inventories her — neck, hair, hand, petticoat — while she pleads a convent retreat; the story grants her no interior, only illumination

reader.subject: char:aunt
reader.to: 'this night of Our Lord': piety meters even a bazaar; the household calendar is liturgical before it is commercial

reader.subject: char:uncle
reader.to: the household's own cheapened Orientalism: 'The Arab's Farewell to his Steed' recited over a forgotten florin — the East as parlour piece, at home before the boy ever boards the train

reader.subject: place:market-streets
reader.to: a come-all-you about O'Donovan Rossa in the market din: nationalist memory hawked alongside pig-cheeks — the political frame the boy's romance screens out
